The town’s clockmaker retired on a Thursday, leaving a note in his window:

**TIME WILL CONTINUE WITHOUT MY ASSISTANCE.**

By Friday, three people had complained.

One said the note was defeatist. One worried about the warranty on her grandfather clock. The third, a boy of nine, wanted to know whether the clockmaker had tested this claim.

“Not thoroughly,” the clockmaker admitted.

So they sat on the bench outside his shop.

A bus arrived late. A dog investigated the base of a lamppost. Across the road, the baker carried out a tray of rolls and burned his thumb exactly as he had every morning for twenty-six years.

“Seems to be working,” the boy said.

“So far.”

The boy had brought a broken wristwatch. Its hands were stopped at 4:17.

“Could you fix this before you stop?”

The clockmaker held it to his ear, then turned it over. The back was scratched almost smooth.

“Yours?”

“My dad’s. He gave it to me when he got one that counts his steps.”

“Does he walk more now?”

“He checks more.”

The clockmaker laughed. He took a small screwdriver from his waistcoat pocket.

“I thought you retired,” the boy said.

“I have.”

“Then why do you still carry that?”

The clockmaker looked at the screwdriver as though it had followed him out of the shop.

“I suppose I haven’t found anywhere else to put it.”

He unlocked the door, and the boy went in after him.
